title: The Diffusion of Mainstream and Disinformation News on Twitter: The Case of Italy and France
screen_reason: Observational Twitter study (Streaming API, one month per country) of tweets carrying links to curated lists of disinformation vs mainstream news outlets in Italy and France. The Conclusion states verbatim the share of shared news that came from disinformation sources - 'approximately 15% of the total share of news in Italy and 10% in France' - a quantitative share with a denominator from behavioural platform data, so SHARING (content_share) is extractable. Not a detection/classifier paper (no model is evaluated), not an intervention or belief study.

estimates.measure_type: % of tweets sharing links to monitored Italian news outlets that pointed to disinformation outlets rather than mainstream outlets
estimates.value_raw: "approximately 15% of the total share of news in Italy" (Table 1: Disinformation 99,569 tweets vs Mainstream 592,463 tweets, i.e. a stated 6:1 mainstream-to-disinformation ratio)
estimates.denominator: All tweets collected in Italy that contained a link to one of the monitored news outlets (99,569 disinformation + 592,463 mainstream = 692,032 news-link tweets from 60+ disinformation and 25 mainstream Italian domains)
estimates.definition: A tweet counted in the numerator if the news URL it carried belonged to one of the 60+ Italian disinformation domains; every article published by such a domain is assumed to be a disinformation article (source-level assignment, no item-level verification).
estimates.misinfo_def: "we use the term disinformation as a short-hand to indicate a broad spectrum of misleading and potentially harmful information, which ranges from false news intended to harm to hyper-partisan stories, click-bait, incorrect news reporting and unverified rumours"
estimates.n: 692,032 news-link tweets (99,569 disinformation + 592,463 mainstream); 11,293 disinformation-sharing and 85,146 mainstream-sharing users
estimates.source_quote: negligible compared to mainstream news, with approximately 15%
estimates.page_loc: §4 Conclusions and Future Directions (p. 621); counts in Table 1 (p. 618)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Source lists, not item coding: 60+ Italian disinformation websites taken from Pierri, Artoni & Ceri (2020), themselves 'compiled by resorting to blacklists on Italian fact-checking websites'; 25 Italian mainstream outlets from Del Vicario et al. (2019), the list 'provided by the association for the verification of newspaper circulation in Italy (Accertamenti Diffusione Stampa)'. No inter-coder reliability applies or is reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: For what concerns the Italian scenario, we referred to [16] to ob- tain a list of 60+ Italian disinformation websites, and to [25] to obtain a list of 25 Italian mainstream outlets;
estimates.notes: The 15 % is stated verbatim in the Conclusion; its base is the tweet volume, since 99,569/(99,569+592,463) = 14.4 %, consistent with the stated 6:1 ratio, whereas the URL base would give 6.1 % and the user base 11.7 %. I kept the paper's own stated figure rather than my recomputation. Denominator is not all Italian news sharing but sharing of the 85 monitored domains, hence denom_selection=curated; denom_scope=news_diet because the denominator is the (shared) news stream rather than a topic. breadth is empty per the schema rule for source-level lists. The author explicitly flags the source-level assumption as imperfect (see item6_quote), which inflates the numerator relative to item-level verification. Described by the author as 'preliminary results from an ongoing investigation'. The PDF's two-column -layout rendering interleaves the left and right columns on every line, so no multi-sentence verbatim span exists in the text file; source_quote is therefore the contiguous line fragment that carries the value. The full conclusion sentence, in reading order, is: "Overall, the amount of misleading and potentially harmful information is small yet not negligible compared to mainstream news, with approximately 15% of the total share of news in Italy and 10% in France."

estimates.measure_type: % of tweets sharing links to monitored French news outlets that pointed to disinformation outlets rather than mainstream outlets
estimates.value_raw: "10% in France" (Table 2: Disinformation 247,173 tweets vs Mainstream 2,125,781 tweets, i.e. a stated 9:1 mainstream-to-disinformation ratio)
estimates.denominator: All tweets collected in France that contained a link to one of the monitored news outlets (247,173 disinformation + 2,125,781 mainstream = 2,372,954 news-link tweets from the Décodex-derived disinformation list and the Top-50 mainstream domains)
estimates.definition: A tweet counted in the numerator if the news URL it carried belonged to a French disinformation domain, defined as a Décodex category (b) 'websites which notably share fake news' or (c) 'websites which are untrustworthy' that generated at least 1 M Facebook engagements in the Le Monde inquiry; satirical sites were excluded. Every article from such a domain is assumed to be a disinformation article.
estimates.misinfo_def: "we use the term disinformation as a short-hand to indicate a broad spectrum of misleading and potentially harmful information, which ranges from false news intended to harm to hyper-partisan stories, click-bait, incorrect news reporting and unverified rumours"
estimates.n: 2,372,954 news-link tweets (247,173 disinformation + 2,125,781 mainstream); 38,938 disinformation-sharing and 425,960 mainstream-sharing users
estimates.source_quote: of the total share of news in Italy and 10% in France.
estimates.page_loc: §4 Conclusions and Future Directions (p. 621); counts in Table 2 (p. 619)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Source lists, not item coding: French disinformation and mainstream outlets taken from a 2018 Le Monde investigation (Senecat) that used Le Monde's Décodex to classify sources as (a) satirical, (b) notably sharing fake news, (c) untrustworthy, (d) credible and reliable; (a) excluded, (b) and (c) with >=1 M Facebook engagements treated as disinformation, and the Top-50 (d) sites by engagement treated as mainstream. No inter-coder reliability applies or is reported.

Not comparable to Italy on equal footing: the author notes the French mainstream volume is partly an artefact of monitoring 50 mainstream sources versus 25 in Italy, so the cross-country difference in the disinformation share is confounded by list size. Same source-level caveat as the Italian row. The PDF's two-column -layout rendering interleaves the left and right columns on every line, so no multi-sentence verbatim span exists in the text file; source_quote is therefore the contiguous line fragment that carries the value. The full conclusion sentence, in reading order, is: "Overall, the amount of misleading and potentially harmful information is small yet not negligible compared to mainstream news, with approximately 15% of the total share of news in Italy and 10% in France." moderator_quote is likewise truncated to one line; the full French source-list paragraph is reproduced in ground_truth_detail.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) the URL-level share (6,732 disinformation of 6,732+103,214 Italian URLs; 28,499 of 28,499+225,304 French URLs) - the percentage is never stated and the denominator would be a cross-category sum I computed, barred by R8. (b) The user-level share (11,293 disinformation-sharing users vs 85,146 mainstream in Italy; 38,938 vs 425,960 in France, reported only as 8:1 and ~'double the number of users compared to Italy') - no valid denominator exists because users who shared both domains appear in both counts (the intersection networks have 9,334 and 31,092 nodes), so no SHARING actor_share row can be built without a computed and double-counting denominator. (c) The diffusion-network indicators in Table 3 (nodes, edges, WCC, GCC share e.g. 82.6 % of the Italian disinformation network in its giant component, clustering, K-core) are network-topology descriptors, not shares of misinformation; the GCC percentages are shares of a network's own nodes and say nothing about prevalence. (d) The polarization index rho = (tm-td)/(tm+td) is shown only as a histogram/KDE (Figure 7) with no share of users above a threshold, so no row. (e) No CONCENTRATION row: the paper says 'only a handful of Italian outlets actively engage with Twitter users' and shows Top-10 source bar charts (Figures 3-6) with axis values only, but never states a top-X%-of-sources to Y%-of-shares pair, so R1 cannot be satisfied. (f) The Reuters Institute Digital News Report figures quoted in the Introduction (40 % of Italians trust news, 23 % trust news on social media, 24 % trust in France, 14 % trust in social media, 8 %/9 % using Twitter for news) are trust and platform-use statistics cited from another source - both out of construct and barred by R8.

rob.design: Convenience census of platform data via curated domain seeds: Twitter Streaming API run continuously for one month per country (Italy 16/11-16/12/2019; France 25/11-25/12/2019), capturing tweets containing URLs from pre-specified outlet lists (Italy: 60+ disinformation domains from fact-checker blacklists, 25 mainstream domains from Accertamenti Diffusione Stampa; France: Décodex-derived (b)+(c) domains with >=1M Facebook engagements, Top-50 (d) mainstream domains). No sampling of users and no survey, so no response rate. Classification is entirely source-level with no item-level coding, no coders and no reliability statistics; the author states the assumption's limits explicitly. The author addresses the Twitter API 1 % rate limit and reports never exceeding it (always <2 x 10^6 tweets/day against a ~5 x 10^8 daily global volume), so no missing-data adjustment was needed. Datasets deposited (tweet IDs only) at https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/CBHUMA. Self-described as preliminary results of an ongoing investigation; a workshop companion paper (6 pages), and cross-country comparison is confounded by unequal mainstream list sizes (25 vs 50). Quote note: the two-column -layout rendering of this PDF interleaves columns line by line, so item6_quote and item10_quote are the longest contiguous verbatim spans available; item6_quote begins mid-word ('tive' from 'deceptive') and its full sentence reads 'In particular, we assume that each article published on the former class is effectively a disinformation article, and likewise for mainstream news, although this might not be always true as deceptive websites do not share solely false stories, and reported case of misleading information on traditional outlets are not rare[12].'
